subject: sociology
chapter_title: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion

concepts.title: Social Inequality and the Three Forms of Capital
concepts.section: 5.1 What Is Social About Social Inequality and Exclusion?
concepts.definition: Social inequality is social in three ways - it divides groups rather than individuals, it is not merely economic even though the two usually travel together, and it is systematic and structured rather than random. Following Bourdieu, valued resources take three forms of capital: economic capital of assets and income, cultural capital of qualifications and status, and social capital of networks of contacts - and each form can be converted into the others, as when a well-off family buys expensive education or influential friends open doors to a well-paid job.
concepts.formula: social_senses = group_not_individual + not_only_economic + systematic_structured ; capitals = economic + cultural + social (convertible)
concepts.key_idea: Hard work matters, but group differences explain why back-breaking labour rarely lifts life chances - no rich man keeps the stone-breaking jobs for himself.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy105.txt, section 5.1 opening and Social Inequality (Bourdieu 1986 three capitals, Activity 5.1 diaries)

solution_steps.action: check the three senses of the social

concepts.title: Social Stratification and Its Three Principles
concepts.definition: Social stratification is the system by which a society ranks categories of people in a hierarchy that shapes identity, relationships and access to resources. Three principles explain it: it belongs to society rather than to individual differences, arising once a surplus exists beyond basic needs; it persists over generations because position is ascribed through the family and protected by endogamous marriage within the caste; and it is propped up by ideology - beliefs such as purity and pollution that make the hierarchy look fair or inevitable, with the privileged defending it most and the humiliated at the bottom likeliest to challenge it.
concepts.key_idea: Birth dictates opportunity in caste, and a hierarchy survives only while enough people see it as legitimate or unavoidable.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy105.txt, Social Stratification (three numbered principles, surplus in advanced societies, endogamy, purity-pollution ideology)

solution_steps.action: check the society-wide and persistence claims

concepts.title: Prejudice, Stereotype, Discrimination and Social Exclusion
concepts.definition: Prejudice is a pre-judgement - an opinion formed before evidence, resting on hearsay and resisting correction, and it may be favourable as well as hostile. Stereotypes are the fixed, inflexible characterisations that feed prejudice, treating a whole community as one person with one trait, as in the colonial labels of martial or cowardly races. Discrimination is prejudice put into behaviour - refusing a job or a house - and is hard to prove because it hides behind claims of merit. Social exclusion is broader still: the systematic, structural cutting off of individuals or groups from full involvement in society, denying access to education, health, transport, banking, social security and even the police or judiciary.
concepts.key_idea: Exclusion is never accidental - it grows from structural features of society, so legislation alone cannot end it without constant social campaigns.

concepts.title: Caste-Based Inequality: Untouchability and the Poverty Tables
concepts.section: 5.2 The Caste System as a Discriminatory System / Untouchability / Tables 1 and 2
concepts.definition: The caste system legitimises discrimination by tying occupation and status to birth; untouchability is its most vicious edge, placing so-called impure castes outside the hierarchy itself, with three dimensions - exclusion, humiliation-subordination and exploitation such as forced unpaid labour. The data confirm the tie of caste to class: in 2011-12, 45.3 per cent of rural Scheduled Tribes lived below the poverty line against an all-group rural average of 25.4, and in 1999-2000 only 1.4 per cent of rural STs were affluent against 31.7 per cent of rural Sikhs - so the privileged remain overwhelmingly upper caste while the disadvantaged cluster in the lower castes.
concepts.key_idea: Distance pollution once punished even a shadow, and Harijan, Dalit and Adivasi each replaced abusive names with terms of dignity and assertion.

concepts.title: Race and Caste Compared: Apartheid Arithmetic
concepts.section: 5.2 Box 5.1b Race and Caste - A Cross-Cultural Comparison
concepts.definition: South Africa's apartheid, law from 1948, stratified society by race much as caste does in India: the white minority of about one in seven denied the Black majority citizenship, land and voice; Black workers earned on average one-fourth of white earnings; and millions were forced into Bantustan homelands covering only 14 per cent of the land while Blacks formed close to 80 per cent of the population. Only in 1994, after decades of struggle under the African National Congress and Nelson Mandela, did Black majority rule arrive, though economic capital remains largely in white hands.
concepts.formula: land_per_head_ratio = homeland_land_share / homeland_population_share ; earnings_multiple = white_earnings / black_earnings
concepts.key_idea: Homelands gave the Black majority less than a fifth of the average land per head, and whites out-earned blacks four to one - the arithmetic of racial caste.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy105.txt, Box 5.1b (apartheid law 1948, one-fourth earnings, 14 per cent land for 80 per cent population, Mandela 1994)
question_patterns: compute how the homeland land share compared with the population share forced to live there under apartheid

solution_steps.action: divide the homeland land share by the Black population share
solution_steps.explain: 14 per cent of the land carried close to 80 per cent of the people, so the quotient shows the land per head relative to the national average

solution_steps.action: divide the white average earnings by the Black average earnings
solution_steps.explain: with Black pay at one-fourth of white pay, the quotient gives the racial earnings multiple

concepts.title: Reservations, Anti-Discrimination Laws and OBC Politics
concepts.section: 5.2 State and Non-State Initiatives / The Other Backward Classes
concepts.definition: The state answers caste discrimination with reservations - seats in legislatures, government jobs and educational institutions set aside for Scheduled Castes and Tribes in proportion to their population share, extended to the Other Backward Classes from the early 1990s. A legal arc runs from the Caste Disabilities Removal Act of 1850, through Article 17 of the 1950 Constitution abolishing untouchability and the 1989 Prevention of Atrocities Act, to the Ninety-Third Amendment of 2005 bringing OBC reservation to higher education. OBC politics itself grew from the sidelined Kaka Kalelkar report of 1953 to the B.P. Mandal Commission, implemented in 1990, turning their roughly 41 per cent share of the national population into national political influence.
concepts.formula: reservation_spheres = legislatures + government_jobs + educational_institutions ; obc_trajectory = kalelkar_1953 sidelined -> mandal_report -> implemented_1990
concepts.key_idea: Laws passed again and again prove that legislation alone cannot end a social practice - Dalit and OBC movements push change from below.

concepts.title: Adivasi Struggles: Forests, Displacement and Identity
concepts.definition: Adivasis, coined in the 1930s to mean original inhabitants, lost their forest rights when the colonial government reserved forests for timber from the late nineteenth century, and independent India's capital-intensive industrialisation then acquired their mineral-rich lands for dams and mines - the Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada and Polavaram on the Godavari displaced hundreds of thousands - a process critics call internal colonialism. Tribal movements against outsiders called dikus and the state won statehood for Jharkhand and Chattisgarh, which adivasis could demand because, unlike Dalits, they were concentrated in contiguous areas.
concepts.formula: adivasi_losses = forest_rights_reserved + land_acquired_for_dams_mines + displacement_without_rehabilitation ; wins = jharkhand + chattisgarh statehood
concepts.key_idea: Being Adivasi names shared experiences of lost forests, alienated land and repeated displacement rather than any ancient essence.

concepts.title: Struggle for Women's Equality and Rights
concepts.section: 5.3 Struggle for women's equality and rights
concepts.definition: Gender inequality is social, not natural - matrilineal societies like the Nairs and Khasis, and African women farmers and traders, prove no biology blocks women's inheritance or leadership. The nineteenth-century middle-class reform movements fought sati under Raja Rammohun Roy, widow remarriage through Ranade, caste-plus-gender oppression through Jyotiba Phule, and Muslim social reform through Sir Syed Ahmed Khan; women themselves wrote back, from Tarabai Shinde's Stree Purush Tulana of 1882 to Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain's Sultana's Dream of 1905, an early feminist science fiction. The 1931 Karachi Session pledged equal rights for women, and the movement re-emerged in the 1970s around modern issues such as media representation, unequal development, legal reform and the falling child sex ratio.
concepts.formula: reform_sites = anti_sati_roy + widow_remarriage_ranade + phule_caste_gender + sir_syed_education ; women_voices = tarabai_1882 + rokeya_1905 ; karachi_1931 = equal_rights_pledge
concepts.key_idea: Once the right to education was conceded, confining women to household curricula became impossible - and the twenty-first century adds new battles like the declining child sex ratio.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy105.txt, section 5.3 (reform movements, Boxes 5.3 and 5.4, Karachi Session declaration, 1970s re-emergence)

concepts.title: Disability as a Social Construction
concepts.definition: The differently abled are disabled not only by impairment but by a society built without them - buildings without ramps, schooling split into segregated streams, courts reached only by stairs. Anita Ghai likens their invisibility to Ellison's Invisible Man; culture deepens it by reading disability as fate or retribution for past karma and labelling people bechara. Replacing crippled or retarded with visually impaired or physically challenged shifts attention to the social model: disablement lies in the construction of society, and disability and poverty feed each other, leaving disabled people among the poorest - which is why Census 2011 widened its count to eight types of disability against five in 2001.
concepts.formula: social_model = society_renders_disabled (built_environment + segregated_schooling + labels) ; poverty_link = disability <-> poverty two_way
concepts.key_idea: We are disabled by steps at the courthouse and by two-stream schooling, not merely by body or fate - and the disabled themselves forced the public rethinking.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy105.txt, section 5.4 (Ghai and Ellison, public perception features, Brisenden quote, Box 5.5 Census 2011 approach, Boxes 5.6 and 5.7)
